newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Labour still odds-on after UK budget.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Labour still odds-on after UK budget.

text.p: The British budget has failed to boost the ruling Conservative government's re-election prospects, with a majority of economists still factoring in a Labour victory, a Reuters poll showed on Wednesday.

While many of the economists reckoned Chancellor Kenneth Clarke could have notched up one or two percentage points in the opinion polls, 34 out of 35 said it would not be enough to get the Conservatives re-elected at the next election.
"Lazarus is not going to rise from the dead on the back of one budget," said John Sheppard, chief economist at Yamaichi.
The Conservatives, lagging way behind opposition Labour in the opinion polls, are striving to claw back some ground by May 22 1997 -- the last possible date for a general election.
Under pressure from his party, Clarke had to balance electorate-wooing tax giveaways with the need for tight fiscal policy for the good of the economy.

"He had a difficult job in terms of needing to satisfy some pressure from his own party for a looser fiscal stance with a macroeconomic need for a tighter one," said David Mackie, economist at JP Morgan. "I think he did as good a job as he could have done under the circumstances."
But despite this being the last budget before an election, it was unlikely to affect voting behaviour, regardless of its contents, economists said.

"They (the government) were caught between a rock and a hard place in the sense that they are significantly behind in the polls and they couldn't do anything in the budget to turn that around," said Stewart Robertson, UK economist at Lombard Street Research.
"Any giveaway would have been crucified by the financial markets and the press," he added.

Yet despite a cautious welcome in the markets, the budget failed to stem worries over interest rate hikes in the near future. The survey showed base rates rising to 6.5 percent by the end of June next year from six percent currently, and advancing to 7.0 percent by the time 1997 is over.

"I dont think (the budget) made any substantial change to the financial position of the personal sector or that of the government themselves to suggest that the interest rate path will be anything but upwards," said Patrick Moon, economic adviser at Lloyds-TSB Group.

Clarke forecast consumer spending growth of more than four percent in 1997 in Tuesday's budget. Economists said that meant monetary policy would have to tighten if Clarke were to meet his inflation target of 2.5 percent for the foreseeable future.

"I think the budget is going to prove a little more inflationary than expected. Combined with expectations of stronger growth next year, rates will have to be raised," said Sharda Persaud, European economist at San Paolo Bank.

And 10-year gilt yields look set to climb, according to the 30 economists who gave forecasts. On average they predict yields to rise steadily from 7.60 percent at the end of this year to 7.95 percent by the end of June as political uncertainties weigh.

"The budget should have provided a catalyst for the gilt market to rally in the near term, but investors are not going to be flocking to buy gilts very close to the election," said David Owen, UK economist at Kleinwort Benson.
The poll showed growth would ease off and gilt yields would end 1997 at around 8.00 percent.
"Once a Labour government is established and announces policies to lower inflation after the election, then we should start to see gilts outperform," Owen said.

While both the conservative and labour parties have said they will hold a referendum to decide if Britain will join European Monetary Union (EMU), Labour is widely seen as the more pro-European of the two, which would account for the forecast tail-off in gilt yields if Labour win.
